brief.request: Fictional public brief: design a one-afternoon London launch pop-up for Rill, an invented lightweight daypack brand. Bonobo means the electronic music artist and is a client-provided research signal, not a verified audience profile. Keep try-on; avoid live performances and forced signup. concepts.title: Load Line: a public swap circuit
concepts.coreClaim: The try-on is taught by comparison: each visitor carries realistic daily loads through the same short circuit in two different packs and feels which one fits better, in public, at their own pace, without booking and without leaving personal data.

mechanism.description: The 80 square metres is divided into five zones in one direction of travel: a payload bay with colour-coded totes (commute, laptop-and-lunch, day out) labelled by weight; a strap-set mirror where a host sets torso and sternum strap length once per visitor; a three-minute circuit of a low step platform, a 20-metre walk lane and a reach-and-squat marker; a swap bench holding a second pack already set to the same strap marks; and an exit board where the visitor pins one paper verdict per pack. The try-on is comparative, semi-public and self-paced: no appointment, no registration or contact details, and the only record is a paper fit card the visitor keeps plus anonymous board entries.
mechanism.organization: Sequenced self-serve try-on circuit with an anonymous shared verdict board

journey.action: Visitor enters without registering, reads a single A1 board explaining the three-step sequence, and picks a payload tote by the kind of day they actually carry.
A host sets torso strap length and sternum strap against the visitor's back and records the settings on a blank fit card.
Visitor walks the step platform, the 20-metre lane and the reach-and-squat marker with the first pack, naming pressure points aloud to a companion or to the host.
At the swap bench the visitor moves the same payload into a second pack pre-set to the same strap marks and repeats the identical route, so load and task stay constant.
Visitor pins one anonymous paper verdict per pack on the exit board, each marked with pack ID and the station where discomfort appeared.
Visitor takes the fit card with both strap settings and the pack IDs they preferred, so the answer to 'which fitted better' survives the walk home.

productTouchpoints: Weight-labelled payload totes in three daily-load profiles
Strap-setting mirror station with a printed torso-length gauge
Three-minute circuit: low step platform, 20 m lane markings, reach-and-squat marker
Swap bench with two packs pre-set to matching strap marks
Anonymous paper verdict slips and pack ID tags
Paper fit card carrying both strap settings
openQuestions: The packs are fictional and unspecified: strap geometry, torso-length range and pack weights must be checked against real samples before the circuit is built, or the comparison teaches nothing reliable.

Whether a step platform, floor lane markings and weighted totes are permitted in the eventual London venue, and what supervision or insurance they require, is unconfirmed; venue and safety conditions remain open.
The circuit assumes visitors arrive in a flow rather than a queue; the effect of waiting beside a public verdict board is unknown, and no attendance figure has been estimated or measured.
Whether an anonymous public board produces honest verdicts when visitors notice others watching has not been tested.

The illustrative GBP 8,000–12,000 envelope has not been quoted against any supplier; totes, printed fit cards, floor graphics, host hours and any platform hire sit inside it as planning assumptions only.
unverifiedEffects: That swapping packs on an identical route makes comfort differences easier to notice and describe is a design assumption, not a measured outcome.
No claim is made about visitor numbers, dwell time, verdict completion, purchase intent, recall or brand affinity; none of these were observed or predicted by the saved evidence.
That daily-load totes matching real commuter weight produce a more truthful fit judgment than an unloaded try-on is untested.
No relationship between this concept and Bonobo, Bonobo's listeners, or the returned brands' customers has been established.

concepts.title: Fit Bench: one-to-one measured try-on
concepts.coreClaim: The try-on is taught as measurement on the visitor's own body inside a 15-minute maximum from arrival to departure: one fitter, one pack, three comfort readings and one recorded strap change, taken in a single private carry that pauses once at a safe stop for the adjustment and never asks the visitor to queue, register or perform for a crowd.

mechanism.description: The 80 square metres is arranged as one private route with no waiting area and no public board: a ready bench holding one pack pre-set to a mid-range torso strap plus one pre-counted day kit (laptop sleeve, bottle, jacket, lunch) laid out flat; a measurement spot on the wall with a height strip and torso-length gauge; a taped safety box that lies off the 20-metre indoor loop, with a stop marker in front of it; and a marked halfway point on the loop. A single fitter runs one visitor through a 15-minute maximum, timed from the moment the visitor steps in and using one timeline throughout. Minutes 0–1.5: briefing, no registration and no obligation to continue, plus confirmation that the visitor may stop at any point. Minutes 1.5–3: torso length and shoulder width measured at the wall and written on the blank fit card, and the pack's torso strap and sternum strap set once and marked in tape. Minutes 3–4.5: the visitor stands still with the loaded pack and the fitter takes reading 1 against named contact points. Minutes 4.5–7: the visitor walks the loop alone at their own pace to the stop marker. Minutes 7–9: the visitor stops still inside the taped safety box, off the loop; the fitter changes exactly one variable (sternum strap position or torso strap length, written down), takes reading 2 standing still, and no strap is touched while the visitor is walking. Minutes 9–10.5: the visitor resumes and walks the remaining loop back to the bench. Minutes 10.5–12: reading 3 standing at the bench, and the visitor adds or removes one item at a time to match their own typical day. Minutes 12–14: the fitter writes the fit card in front of the visitor (measured torso length, the one change, all three readings, the visitor's notes). Minutes 14–15: handover and questions, with one minute of buffer so the session ends by 15 at the latest and can end earlier at any point. The try-on stays conversational and private; no contact details are collected or retained, and the only record is the handwritten card the visitor keeps.
mechanism.organization: Private one-to-one try-on bench with a 15-minute maximum session and one safe walking stop

journey.action: Visitor steps straight onto the start point with no queuing; the fitter states that this is a 15-minute maximum, single-visitor try-on with no registration, no contact details and no obligation to continue, and that the visitor may stop at any time.

Fitter measures torso length and shoulder width at the wall gauge, writes the numbers on the blank fit card in view of the visitor, and sets the pre-fitted pack's torso strap and sternum strap once, marking both in tape.
Visitor stands still at the bench with the pack loaded with the pre-counted standard day kit, and the fitter takes comfort reading 1 against named contact points.
Visitor walks the marked 20-metre loop alone at their own pace and comes to a full stop at the stop marker in front of the taped safety box, off the route.

Visitor stays rooted inside the safety box; the fitter changes exactly one variable — sternum strap position or torso strap length — writes it on the card, and takes reading 2 standing still. No strap is touched while the visitor is moving.
Visitor resumes walking and completes the remaining loop back to the bench.
Fitter takes reading 3 standing at the bench and the visitor adds or removes one item at a time from the day kit to match their own typical day.
Fitter writes the fit card in front of the visitor: measured torso length, the one recorded change, all three readings and the visitor's own notes. No contact details are kept.
Visitor takes the handwritten card and the fitter answers remaining questions; one minute of buffer means the session ends by 15 at the latest and may end earlier at any point.

productTouchpoints: Measurement wall with height strip and torso-length gauge
Low fitting bench holding one pre-fitted pack at a time
Pre-counted standard day kit laid out flat, adjusted one item at a time
Tape markers on torso strap and sternum strap, re-set once while the visitor stands still
Floor-marked 20-metre loop with a stop marker in front of a taped safety box set off the route
Contact-point diagram the fitter uses to name readings, shown to the visitor at each standing reading
Blank handwritten fit card written up in front of the visitor in the last minutes of the session
openQuestions: Whether the minute split from briefing to handover can actually be held inside 15 minutes with an unfamiliar pack is unverified; it is a planning estimate, not a rehearsed schedule.

Whether the fitter can make one strap change and take reading 2 at the stop marker, inside the taped safety box, in two minutes without the visitor leaving it or another visitor walking into the stop zone is untested.
Whether a short measurement and a 1.5-minute briefing is enough for a first-time visitor to give an informed reading is untested.

The packs are fictional and unspecified: strap geometry, torso-length range and pack weights must be checked against real samples, and whether the halfway stop marker and safety box can be placed without blocking the entrance or an emergency route is unconfirmed.
What the room does with a visitor arriving while a session is running is unresolved, since the waiting bench has been removed and there is no booking or queue system.
The three reading protocols and the named contact points are a designer's proposal, not a validated fit method, and the shorter timing could make them less reliable.
Exact venue, insurance, floor loading, floor taping or fixing and any supervision or safety conditions are unconfirmed.
Whether visitors accept a no-data, handwritten-record try-on rather than a digital one has not been tested.
unverifiedEffects: That three readings compressed into a 15-minute maximum still produce an accurate comfort judgment is an assumption; no comfort, fit-accuracy or learning effect was measured, and the shorter timing may reduce it.
That one mid-walk stop, with a single strap change made while the visitor stands still, is enough to let a visitor separate the effect of that change from the effect of resuming walking is untested.
Whether stopping and resuming breaks the rhythm of the carry and weakens the comparison, or makes the change easier to notice, is unknown.

Whether 15 minutes per fitter works as an afternoon throughput or becomes a bottleneck is unknown; the shorter session may serve more visitors or may simply compress the experience, and no attendance figure has been estimated or measured.
That removing the waiting bench and the longer walk preserves the private, unhurried quality of the one-to-one try-on is a design argument, not an observed preference.
No claim is made about dwell time, conversion, trust, recall or repeat visits, and none of these were returned by the saved evidence.
No relationship between this concept and Bonobo, its listeners, or the returned brands' customers has been established.

revisions.summary: Draft 2 fixes the two flagged problems in the Fit Bench concept. It uses one timeline in every field, with identical stage boundaries: briefing 0–1.5, measure and set straps 1.5–3, reading 1 standing 3–4.5, walk to the stop marker 4.5–7, walk halted for the single one-variable adjustment and reading 2 7–9, walk resumed to the bench 9–10.5, reading 3 10.5–12, writing the fit card 12–14, and a one-minute handover buffer that ends at 15 at the latest. No strap is touched while the visitor is moving: the visitor stops in a taped safety box off the loop, the fitter makes one recorded change, reading 2 is taken standing still, and the visitor then resumes. The privacy format, three readings, the single locked title and the brief constraints are unchanged. Feasibility, the minute split and the learning value are still marked unverified. Concept A is untouched, no Qloo query was made, and no evidence link was changed.
impact: Only the selected concept Fit Bench changes; concept A (Load Line), the brief and all evidence links are untouched.
The locked title is preserved and not submitted as an edit.
The private one-fitter, one-visitor, one-pack format, the no-registration and no-contact-details rule, and the three readings are preserved.

Mechanism and journey now share identical minute boundaries: 0–1.5 briefing, 1.5–3 measure and set straps, 3–4.5 reading 1, 4.5–7 walk to the stop marker, 7–9 stopped adjustment and reading 2, 9–10.5 walk to the bench, 10.5–12 reading 3 and load check, 12–14 write the fit card, 14–15 handover and buffer.

The strap change and reading 2 now happen with the visitor standing still inside a taped safety box off the loop; the earlier 'without stopping the walk' wording is removed from the claim, mechanism, journey, touchpoints and effects.
The fit card is now written inside the timeline rather than left to the visitor afterwards.
Removing the waiting bench and the longer walk frees floor space but removes the in-session buffer for arrivals.
No Qloo query was made and no evidence was added, removed or revalidated.
unknowns: Whether the planning minute split holds inside 15 minutes from arrival to departure with an unfamiliar pack is unverified.
Whether one strap change and reading 2 can be completed in two minutes at the stop marker without the visitor or another visitor crossing the stop zone is untested.
Whether the shorter, interrupted carry still teaches fit and carrying comfort as well as a longer session is untested.
Whether 15 minutes per fitter helps or hurts afternoon throughput, and how the room absorbs arrivals with no waiting bench and no booking, is unknown.
Rill's fictional pack adjustment range and whether the taped safety box and stop marker can be placed without obstructing entry or an emergency route are unconfirmed.
Venue, supervision, insurance, floor taping and safety conditions remain unconfirmed.

Minutes 3–4.5: the visitor stands still with the loaded pack and the fitter takes reading 1 against named contact points. Minutes 4.5–7: the visitor walks the loop alone at their own pace to the stop marker. Minutes 7–9: the visitor stops still inside the taped safety box, off the loop; the fitter changes exactly one variable (sternum strap position or torso strap length, written down), takes reading 2 standing still, and no strap is touched while the visitor is walking. Minutes 9–10.5: the visitor resumes and walks the remaining loop back to the bench. Minutes 10.5–12: reading 3 standing at the bench, and the visitor adds or removes one item at a time to match their own typical day. Minutes 12–14: the fitter writes the fit card in front of the visitor (measured torso length, the one change, all three readings, the visitor's notes). Minutes 14–15: handover and questions, with one minute of buffer so the session ends by 15 at the latest and can end earlier at any point. The try-on stays conversational and private; no contact details are collected or retained, and the only record is the handwritten card the visitor keeps.

before.action: Visitor takes one of two waiting seats and the fitter explains that this is a 30-minute, single-visitor try-on with no registration and no obligation to continue.
Fitter measures torso length and shoulder width at the wall gauge and writes the numbers on a blank fit card, visible to the visitor throughout.
Visitor chooses what goes in the pack from a standard day kit (laptop sleeve, water bottle, jacket, lunch) and adds or removes items to match their own typical day.
Visitor sits and stands at the bench wearing the pack, and the fitter records the first comfort reading against named contact points rather than a single score.
Visitor walks a 20-metre indoor loop alone for around ten minutes, then returns, so nobody is watching or timing them for an audience.
Fitter takes two further readings and changes only the torso strap position, or only the sternum strap, so the visitor feels one cause at a time.
before.stage: Second and third readings, one adjustment

before.action: Visitor leaves with the handwritten card: measured torso length, the strap settings that read most comfortable, and their own notes, with no contact details kept.

after.action: Visitor steps straight onto the start point with no queuing; the fitter states that this is a 15-minute maximum, single-visitor try-on with no registration, no contact details and no obligation to continue, and that the visitor may stop at any time.

Fitter measures torso length and shoulder width at the wall gauge, writes the numbers on the blank fit card in view of the visitor, and sets the pre-fitted pack's torso strap and sternum strap once, marking both in tape.
Visitor stands still at the bench with the pack loaded with the pre-counted standard day kit, and the fitter takes comfort reading 1 against named contact points.
Visitor walks the marked 20-metre loop alone at their own pace and comes to a full stop at the stop marker in front of the taped safety box, off the route.

Visitor stays rooted inside the safety box; the fitter changes exactly one variable — sternum strap position or torso strap length — writes it on the card, and takes reading 2 standing still. No strap is touched while the visitor is moving.
Visitor resumes walking and completes the remaining loop back to the bench.
Fitter takes reading 3 standing at the bench and the visitor adds or removes one item at a time from the day kit to match their own typical day.
Fitter writes the fit card in front of the visitor: measured torso length, the one recorded change, all three readings and the visitor's own notes. No contact details are kept.
Visitor takes the handwritten card and the fitter answers remaining questions; one minute of buffer means the session ends by 15 at the latest and may end earlier at any point.

before: Whether a 30-minute single-visitor try-on per fitter fits an afternoon flow is unknown; how many fitters are needed, and how the room absorbs a queue without turning the bench into a public spectacle, is unresolved.
The seated-and-standing reading protocol and named contact points are a designer's proposal, not a validated fit method; they need checking against how Rill's samples actually adjust.
The fictional packs' adjustment range may not cover real torso-length variation, which would quietly exclude visitors instead of teaching them anything.
Exact venue, insurance, floor loading and any furniture fixing or safety conditions are unconfirmed.
Whether visitors accept a no-data, handwritten-record try-on rather than a digital one has not been tested.
after: Whether the minute split from briefing to handover can actually be held inside 15 minutes with an unfamiliar pack is unverified; it is a planning estimate, not a rehearsed schedule.

Whether the fitter can make one strap change and take reading 2 at the stop marker, inside the taped safety box, in two minutes without the visitor leaving it or another visitor walking into the stop zone is untested.
Whether a short measurement and a 1.5-minute briefing is enough for a first-time visitor to give an informed reading is untested.

The packs are fictional and unspecified: strap geometry, torso-length range and pack weights must be checked against real samples, and whether the halfway stop marker and safety box can be placed without blocking the entrance or an emergency route is unconfirmed.
What the room does with a visitor arriving while a session is running is unresolved, since the waiting bench has been removed and there is no booking or queue system.
The three reading protocols and the named contact points are a designer's proposal, not a validated fit method, and the shorter timing could make them less reliable.
Exact venue, insurance, floor loading, floor taping or fixing and any supervision or safety conditions are unconfirmed.
Whether visitors accept a no-data, handwritten-record try-on rather than a digital one has not been tested.

before: That three timed readings produce a more accurate comfort judgment than one unloaded try-on is an assumption; no comfort, fit-accuracy or learning effect was measured.
No claim is made about dwell time, conversion, trust, recall or repeat visits, and none of these were returned by the saved evidence.
That private one-to-one attention suits this audience better than a public circuit is a design argument, not an observed preference; the Bonobo association says nothing about it.

after: That three readings compressed into a 15-minute maximum still produce an accurate comfort judgment is an assumption; no comfort, fit-accuracy or learning effect was measured, and the shorter timing may reduce it.

Whether stopping and resuming breaks the rhythm of the carry and weakens the comparison, or makes the change easier to notice, is unknown.

Whether 15 minutes per fitter works as an afternoon throughput or becomes a bottleneck is unknown; the shorter session may serve more visitors or may simply compress the experience, and no attendance figure has been estimated or measured.
That removing the waiting bench and the longer walk preserves the private, unhurried quality of the one-to-one try-on is a design argument, not an observed preference.
